```{=html} ``` Linux is often used to be able to analyse large amounts of data. Whenever the data comes from a biological source, we call this type of analysis bioinformatics. There are a number of common files that are used in many of the different types of analysis. We have seen two of them, FASTQ and BED files are both common files for bioinformatics analysis.\ Many of the most common types of file that you will have to work with as a bioinformatician take the form of structured text files, examples include: - Standard formats for representing raw sequences - [FASTA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FASTA_format) - [FASTQ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FASTQ_format) - Tabular formats for representing aligned reads or genome features - [BED](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BED_(file_format)) - [GTF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_transfer_format) - [SAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAM_(file_format)) These types of files have very specific formats, which make sure that we always know what files should look like, tools can recognize the files, and all in all it makes life easier. Some tools in bioinformatics are very specific to accomplish specific tasks. ## Tools For today, we will look at a fairly typical task within bioinformatics, which is aligning reads to an existing reference genome. To simplify things, the following choices about the analysis have been make: 1. We will skip any pre-processing of reads, even though they might contain adapter sequences or low quality data. 1. **STAR** will be used for aligning reads, this is a very popular aligner for RNA-seq data. Many different tools are available, but most of the tools will produce **SAM** files are outputs. 1. The **samtools** package will be used to view and summarize the produced **SAM** files. Again other toolkits are available, however **samtools** is a very popular and often used tool. 1. Finally, **bedtools** will be used to look at reads mapping to gene regions of the reference genome. By default, these tools are not installed on Linux servers and have to be installed separately. ## Analysis First, lets take a look at the files. These files are in the `yeast_files` directory. The reference genome is captured in the `yeast_genome.fasta`, which contains the sequence, and the `yeast_genes.bed` file, which contains the annotation of gene locations. :::: challenge

Challenge:

Print the first 5 lines for each of the reference genome files.
Solution ::: solution

Solution:

To get the first 5 lines of a file, we can use the `head` command. ``` bash cd ~/Intro_to_Linux/yeast_files/ head -n 5 yeast_genome.fasta head -n 5 yeast_genes.bed ``` :::
:::: \ The first column of the BED file refers to the chromosome name, and in the FASTA file the name behind the `>` symbol refers to the name of the chromosome. As you can see, there is a discrepancy between the file and the names for the chromosome. Therefore, we need to fix that before we can move on. The easiest fix is to remove `chr` from the BED file. For this, the command `sed` can be used, which can replace patterns in a file with another piece of text. For example: ``` bash sed "s/^chr//" yeast_genes.bed > yeast_genes_fixed.bed ``` In the command above, the pattern between the first two `/` is the text we want to replace, the text between the second and third `/` is the replacement text. The results are then written to the `yeast_genes_fixed.bed`. To confirm the replacement has worked, lets run the `head` command again. ``` bash head -n 5 yeast_genes_fixed.bed ``` This only confirms it for the first few lines. To check throughout the file, there are a number of different commands that will be helpful. To look at only 1 column within a file, the `cut` command will come in handy. Once the first column is selected, the `sort` and `uniq` are extremely useful to summarize the results: ``` bash cut -f 1 yeast_genes_fixed.bed | sort | uniq ``` Showing us what the unique values that are in the first column. :::: challenge

Challenge:

Explore the command. Make sure you understand the different steps taken. See if you can count the number of genes for each chromosome. *Hint: take a look at the `uniq` command, it has an option to count values*
Solution ::: solution

Solution:

To get the first 5 lines of a file, we can use the `head` command. ``` bash uniq --help ``` The `uniq` command has an option `-c`. If we add that to the command, it should give us a count of each chromosome. ``` bash cut -f 1 yeast_genes_fixed.bed | sort | uniq -c ``` :::
:::: \ The files are now setup to get started with our analysis. This is just an example of some of the commands you will come across when doing bioinformatics. **Note:** This is not a full pipeline, in some of our future training days we will go through how to do specific analyses. To be able to map reads against a reference genome, the genome has to be indexed. Indexing is used by mappers to make mapping faster and easier. Most tools that do mapping will have the option to create an index. The command to create an index for `STAR` will need a specific folder to save the index in. The command is the following: ``` bash mkdir star_index STAR --runThreadN 5 --runMode genomeGenerate --genomeDir ./star_index --genomeFastaFiles ./yeast_genome.fasta --genomeSAindexNbases 10 ``` Once the index has been created, the reads can be mapped against the genome. The command will need links to the index folder and the raw reads to be able to map them correctly. Many commands can run on multiple cpus or threads. We will look more into how to determine how many you can use later, for now it can be set to 2 threads. \ The output is an `BAM` file, which is the binary version of a `SAM` file. It contains the information of how reads are mapped. ``` bash STAR --genomeDir ./star_index/ --readFilesIn ./raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.fastq.gz --runThreadN 2 --outFileNamePrefix raw_yeast_rnaseq_data. --outSAMtype BAM SortedByCoordinate --readFilesCommand 'gunzip -c' ``` To get an idea of how many of the reads have mapped to the reference genome, `samtools` can be used to get a general overview. ``` bash samtools flagstat raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.Aligned.sortedByCoord.out.bam ``` From the results we can see that 100% of the reads have mapped against the reference genome. Many of the reads have secondary locations were the reads map, meaning that a read has two location on the genome where it mapped. For RNA data this is a normal occurrence. \ \ To look at how much of the genome is covered, `bedtools` is the perfect tool to use. ``` bash bedtools genomecov -ibam raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.Aligned.sortedByCoord.out.bam -bg > raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.genomecov.bg ``` Follow by a second command to see how many of the reads are mapped against gene regions. ``` bash bedtools intersect -c -a yeast_genes_fixed.bed -b raw_yeast_rnaseq_data.Aligned.sortedByCoord.out.bam > raw_yeast_overlap_data.bed ``` Within this file, for each gene the amount of reads mapping against it is captured in the 7th column. :::: challenge

Challenge:

What is the maximum amount of reads mapping to a gene? *Hint: Use the `cut` and `sort` commands, check the `--help` of `sort` to see how to sort numeric values.*
Solution ::: solution

Solution:

Using `cut` we can extract the 7th column and then sort them by number. ``` bash sort --help cut -f 7 raw_yeast_overlap_data.bed | sort -n ``` The maximum count is 3,730 reads. :::
:::: \ :::: challenge

Challenge:

Can you find out which gene has this amount of reads mapping against it? The name of the gene is captured in column 4. *Hint: Use `grep`*
Solution ::: solution

Solution:

Using `grep` we can extract the exact number. ``` bash grep "3730" raw_yeast_overlap_data.bed ``` There are different lines that contain this number, but only one in the last column, which is for the gene "RDN37-2". :::
:::: \ ## Threads Now, as mentioned, many of the commands run within bioinformatics can run on multiple threads (also referred to as cpus). Every computer has them, but processes need to share them. Which mean that if we are working on a server, we need to make sure that the commands being run aren't claiming all the threads that are available. \ To check how many processes are currently running, there are two commands to use: - `top` shows all active processes - `htop` gives a user friendly representation of the processes currently running along with CPU and memory usage on the server :::: challenge

Challenge:

Using `htop`, can you see how many tasks are running?
Solution ::: solution

Solution:

There should be a line which says how many tasks are currently running. The screen also shows how much memory is being used. :::
:::: \ Before running any process, it is good to check what the status of the system is. ## AWK Lastly, one powerful command line tool that can be very helpful, though somewhat complex, is `awk`. It can help analyse, filter or manipulate structured files. Lets look at an example to see if we can use `awk` to find out the longest genes within our genome. Gene length isn't captured within the BED file, however the start and stop position are given. To find the longest genes, the follow command will give us the top 10 longest genes. ``` bash awk -F'\t' -v OFS='\t' '{print $4,$3-$2}' yeast_genes_fixed.bed | sort -k2,2nr | head ``` Lets break down the command, because this is complex. - `-F '\t'` sets what the separator is within the file. This is the character which is between the columns. `\t` as we saw at regular expressions means `tab`. - `-v OFS='\t'` tells `awk` that the output should be `tab` separated as well - `'{print $4,$3-$2}'` is where the magic happens. `awk` processes every line of a file one by one. It separates the all the columns and renames them to `$1`, `$2`, etc to the last column index. This means we can make changes to the order, but also do calculations with the different columns. If we substract the start position of our gene from the stop position, it will give the gene length. What this means for this part of the command is that it will report the 4th column followed by the stop column minus the start column. - `sort -k2,2nr` will sort the resulting list. `-k2` specifies the list should be sorted by the second column, and `2nr` specifies that the second column is numeric and it should be sorted in the reverse order. If `awk` is of interest to you, take a look at [Effective AWK Programming](https://www.gnu.org/software/gawk/manual/). Don't worry if this looks extremely complex, this is an advanced Linux command that will become more useful as you get into more difficult challenges.
